entries.narration: Let's start with a question that decides almost everything later: who is responsible for what. Cloud computing is renting capacity that you control through an API, and the useful way to compare the options is to ask how much of the stack you still operate yourself. Take our online shop. If we run it on a virtual machine, that is infrastructure as a service. Azure runs the hardware and the hypervisor, but we install the operating system, patch it, and run the web server. If we deploy the same code to App Service, that is platform as a service. Now Azure patches the operating system and runs the runtime, and we own our code and its configuration. A finished product like Microsoft 365 is software as a service, where we only configure it. Read the table across and the boundary slides to the right as more is managed for you. But look at the top row: your data, your accounts and who can reach them stay yours in every column. That row is why the next chapters spend so long on access. The exact line differs by service, so check each one's documentation. First, though, where does all of this physically live?

Every resource you create lands in a region, which is a geographic area containing Azure datacenters. You choose it, and the choice matters, because the services, machine sizes and prices on offer differ from region to region. Many regions are further divided into availability zones. Each zone is a physically separate location with its own power, cooling and networking, so a fault in one should not take down the others. Some services are zone-redundant, meaning Azure spreads them across zones for you, while others are zonal, meaning you pin an instance to a particular zone. In the diagram our order API runs three instances, one per zone. If a whole zone fails, two instances keep serving. Notice what this does and does not protect against. It is a defence against a datacenter-scale failure. It does nothing about a bad deployment that ships to all three instances, or someone deleting the database. And a second region is a separate boundary again, which only exists if you build it. Next, how resources are grouped and owned.

Three words get mixed up constantly, so let's separate them. A tenant is your organisation's identity directory in Microsoft Entra. It holds users, groups and applications. A subscription is where resources are billed and where quotas apply, and it also acts as a scope for access. Each subscription trusts exactly one tenant, and one tenant can have many subscriptions. The resources themselves live in subscriptions, not in the tenant, and quotas apply per subscription and per region. In the diagram, contoso has a production subscription and a separate development one, so a mistake in dev cannot touch the production bill or its quota. Inside a subscription, a resource group holds resources that share a lifecycle. You create them together, manage them together and, when the time comes, delete them together. Every resource belongs to exactly one group. Here is the misconception to avoid. A resource group is a management container, not a network boundary. Resources in the same group can be in different regions and different networks, and resources in different groups can talk to each other freely. With ownership mapped, how does a request to change any of this actually work?

Whether you click in the portal, type a command in the CLI, call an SDK, or deploy a template, you are doing the same thing underneath. You are sending a management request to Azure Resource Manager, usually shortened to ARM. ARM is the front door. It confirms who you are, checks that you are allowed to perform the operation, applies governance rules such as Azure Policy, and then hands the request to a resource provider. A resource provider is the part of a service that owns one kind of resource. Microsoft.Web handles web apps, Microsoft.Sql handles databases, and Microsoft.Storage handles storage accounts. A provider has to be registered in your subscription before you can create its resources, which is why a brand-new subscription sometimes complains about an unregistered provider on first use. That single path gives one place for access checks, policy and audit. One boundary to remember: this whole path is the control plane, the place where resources are created, changed and deleted. Reading the contents of a blob or running a query against a database does not travel through ARM. We will give that distinction its own section in the next chapter. Now let's make one real request.

Time to make a real request. You can work in the portal, which is good for exploring, or in the Azure CLI, which is better for anything you want to repeat. Cloud Shell gives you the CLI in a browser tab, already signed in. In the code card, the first command picks the development subscription, and the second creates a resource group called rg-retail-dev in Sweden Central, tagged with the environment and an owner. The command sends a request to Resource Manager, and the reply comes back as JSON. We have trimmed it to the fields that matter. The provisioning state says Succeeded, which tells us the group now exists and nothing more. Run the same command again with the same values and you get the same group back rather than a duplicate. The most useful field is the id. A resource ID is a path that reads from broad to specific: the subscription, then the resource group, then the provider, then the resource type and name. For a web app it would pass through Microsoft.Web and the sites type. Because it names exactly one resource, the ID is what policies, role assignments and templates use to point at things. One last topic before we leave foundations: what all of this costs, and how to stop paying for it.

The last foundation is money. Most Azure resources bill for as long as they exist, by time, by size, or by usage. That leads to a classic surprise, shown in our hypothetical ledger. We delete the web app, but the App Service plan it ran on is a separate resource and keeps billing. An unattached disk keeps billing. A public IP address and the logs we collected do too. Four habits help. First, tags. A tag is a name and value pair, like env equals dev, and it makes cost reports filterable by owner or purpose. Tags are not automatically copied from a resource group to the resources inside it, so you apply them deliberately or enforce them with policy. Second, budgets. A budget sends an alert as spending approaches a threshold you choose, but it is not a spending cap. Your resources keep running and keep billing after the alert. Third, review: ask the owner regularly whether the thing is still needed. Fourth, cleanup. Putting a throwaway environment in its own resource group means you can delete the whole group, after checking that nothing else depends on it. That completes the foundations: we know where things live and who pays. Next comes the harder question of who is allowed to do what, which is identity, access and governance.

Everything in Azure begins with a question: who is asking? Proving that is authentication, and it is a separate job from authorisation, which decides what that person may do. In our retail company, Priya works on the support team. She signs in to a Microsoft Entra tenant, the directory we met in the last chapter. Entra checks her credential, which might be a password, a passkey, or a prompt from an authenticator app. Multi-factor authentication asks for a second proof, so a stolen password on its own is not enough. Some organisations prefer that people keep using their corporate account, and that works through federation: Entra trusts another identity provider, and once that provider confirms who Priya is, Entra still issues the token. Conditional Access adds rules, such as requiring multi-factor authentication from an unfamiliar location, but it depends on licensing, so check your plan. Now the key point. The result of all this is a token, a signed proof of identity. A valid token says who Priya is. It grants her nothing yet. What applications get from tokens comes next.

People are not the only ones who need identities. Applications do too, and Entra gives them two related objects. An app registration is the definition of an application: its name, its identifiers, and the permissions it asks for. A service principal is that application's identity inside one specific tenant, and it is the service principal that role assignments and consent attach to. When the order service needs to call the fulfilment API, it proves itself to Entra, often with a certificate or a client secret, and receives an access token for that API. The card shows the token decoded, with made-up values. The audience claim names the API the token is meant for. The issuer and tenant say who vouched for it. The roles claim lists the application permissions it carries, and the expiry says when it stops working. Two cautions. A secret or certificate stored in the application is itself a credential that must be protected and rotated. And decoding a token to read it is not the same as validating it: the receiving API must check the signature, the audience and the expiry. Managed identities remove the secret problem, which we turn to next.

Secrets in code are a liability, so Azure offers a better arrangement: the managed identity. It is a service principal whose credentials Azure creates, stores and rotates on your behalf, and your code never sees a password. There are two kinds. A system-assigned identity is created together with one resource, such as a web app, and deleted when that resource is deleted. It belongs to that one resource only. A user-assigned identity is a standalone resource with its own lifecycle. In the diagram, the order API and a function app both use the same one, called id-retail, and it survives if either of them is removed. The code card shows how little the application needs. The default credential class asks the hosting platform for a token, and the client library presents that token to Blob Storage. Notice what is missing: no key, no connection string. But here is the catch. A managed identity is only an identity. If it has not been given a suitable role on the storage account, the token proves who the app is, and the request is still refused. Granting roles is what role-based access control is for.

Azure role-based access control answers the authorisation question with a simple formula. A role assignment is a principal, a role, and a scope. The principal is the who: a user, a group, or an application identity. The role is a named bundle of allowed actions, such as Reader, which can view resources, or Contributor, which can change them but cannot manage access. Owner can also manage access, which is why it should be rare. The scope is the where, and scopes nest: a management group contains subscriptions, a subscription contains resource groups, and a resource group contains resources. An assignment made at one level applies to everything beneath it. The matrix shows four assignments. The retail developers get Contributor on the development group, but only Reader on production. The auditors get Reader on the whole production subscription, and the web app's identity gets a data role on one storage account. What a principal can do is the sum of all the assignments that reach the resource. So the habit is: assign to groups rather than individuals, and at the narrowest scope that works. One catch remains, and it surprises almost everyone: which kinds of access these roles control.

Here is the idea behind some of the most confusing errors in Azure. Many resources have two doors. The control plane is for managing the resource itself: creating it, configuring it, deleting it. Those requests go through Azure Resource Manager, and management roles like Contributor apply. The data plane is for using what the resource holds, such as reading a blob or sending a message. Those requests go to the service directly, and they are governed by data roles. In the diagram, Priya has Contributor on the storage account. She can create a container without any trouble, because that is a management action. But when she downloads a blob using her own sign-in, the service answers with a 403 and an authorisation permission mismatch, because Contributor contains no data action that allows reading blobs. The fix is not a more powerful management role. It is a data role, such as Blob Data Reader, assigned to the identity at a suitable scope. One more subtlety deserves a warning. Contributor is allowed to list the storage account keys, and keys bypass roles entirely. That is one reason to prefer identity-based access and to disable key access where you can.

Role-based access control says who may act. Azure Policy answers a different question: what state may resources be in? A policy definition is a rule shaped like if this, then that. In the card, if a resource's location is not Sweden Central or North Europe, then the effect is deny. A definition does nothing until it is assigned to a scope, and from then on everything beneath that scope is evaluated. The effect decides what happens. Audit simply flags the resource and allows it. Deny rejects a create or update request that would break the rule. Modify can add or change fields, such as a missing tag, and deploy-if-not-exists can add a companion resource, such as diagnostic settings. Afterwards, compliance reporting shows which resources pass and which do not. A new deny rule does not delete resources that already exist; it marks them non-compliant, and remediation tasks can fix those where the effect supports it. Keep the two systems apart: a person with Owner can still be stopped by policy, and a compliant resource is not proof that the application on it is secure. Next, where do we assign these rules and roles so they apply consistently?

Once a company has more than a handful of subscriptions, assigning roles and policies one at a time stops working. Management groups solve that. They sit above subscriptions and form a hierarchy, and anything assigned to a management group is inherited by every subscription and resource beneath it. In the diagram, a platform group holds the shared subscriptions, such as the hub network and monitoring, while a landing-zones group holds the workload subscriptions, production and development. The allowed-regions policy is assigned once, at landing zones, and both workload subscriptions inherit it. That is one assignment instead of several copies that can drift apart. Splitting production and development into different subscriptions also gives each its own role assignments, policies, quotas and bill, which limits the blast radius of a mistake. Be careful what that claim covers, though. A separate subscription is not automatically a network boundary. If the environments are connected by peering, or share an identity with broad roles, they can still affect each other. Organise management groups around what needs the same policy, not around the company's org chart, and keep the hierarchy shallow. Last in this chapter: privileged access and who owns which layer.

The most powerful roles deserve the strictest handling. The common pattern is just-in-time elevation. Instead of someone holding Owner all day, every day, they are eligible for the role. When they genuinely need it, they activate it, which can require multi-factor authentication, a written reason, and sometimes an approver. The access then lasts for a set time and expires on its own. In Entra this is Privileged Identity Management, and it needs a qualifying licence, so verify your plan before you design around it. Access also rots. People change teams but keep their roles, which is why access reviews exist: owners are periodically asked to re-confirm who still needs what, and stale access is removed. The last piece is ownership. In a landing-zone design, the platform team owns policy, the hub network and identity foundations, and each application team owns the resources inside its own subscription. That boundary only helps if it is written down, and if evidence supports it: the Activity Log and sign-in logs show who did what and when. With ownership and access settled, we can follow a small application onto managed hosting in the next chapter.

We will follow one small application for the whole chapter, so let's start with what it actually does. A browser sends an HTTP request: a method, a path, some headers, and sometimes a body. The hostname gets the request to our app, and the path decides which handler answers. In the code card, the handler for slash products slash 42 is a function inside a long-running process. That process starts once, then waits for requests, and that matters, because it explains where configuration lives. The catalogue address is read from an environment variable at startup, not typed into the code, so the same code can run in development and production with different settings. Now look at the handler itself. To answer, it calls another service, the catalogue store. That dependency call is where most real failures appear: a timeout, a refused connection, an unexpected answer. So when a request fails, the question is not only whether our code ran, but what it was talking to. A 500 tells us our code failed. A timeout does not even tell us whether the dependency did its work. Next, where does this process run?

App Service is Azure's managed home for web applications, and its key idea is the split between a plan and an app. The plan is the compute. It fixes the region, the operating system, the size of the machine, and how many instances you run. The app is your code running on that plan. In the diagram, three apps share one plan: the shop site, the order API and an admin tool. They share the same CPU and memory, which is economical, but it also means a busy app can slow its neighbours. Billing follows the plan, not each app, so a plan costs the same whether it hosts one app or five. The plan also fixes a few choices. You pick Linux or Windows, and a runtime stack such as Python, with a supported version. Versions retire over time, so check support before you commit. The pricing tier matters too, because it sets the size and decides which features exist. Deployment slots, autoscale and some networking options all depend on the tier, so always check eligibility rather than assuming. Now let's put code onto a plan.

Here is the whole journey in four commands. The first creates a Linux plan on the Basic tier. The second creates the web app on that plan and picks a Python runtime. The third sets an app setting, the catalogue address. The fourth deploys a zip file, which is our release artefact: the exact bundle of code we want to run. Now look at what happens on the instance. The platform unpacks the artefact, makes the app settings available as environment variables, and runs a start command to launch the process. The app is only healthy once that process is listening on the port the platform expects. When an app will not start, this sequence tells you where to look. The startup logs usually show it: a setting that is missing, a start command that points at the wrong file, or a process that listens somewhere else. A good habit follows from this. Deploy the same artefact to every environment, and let only the settings differ. Then a bug in production can be reproduced with the same bits. Now, about those settings that hold secrets.

Some settings are secrets, such as a database password, and we do not want them sitting in our settings in plain text. A Key Vault reference helps. Instead of the password, the app setting holds a pointer to a secret in Key Vault. When the app starts, the App Service platform resolves the pointer for us, using the app's managed identity, which we met in the last chapter. The application never knows any of this. It just reads an ordinary environment variable. Two things have to be right for that to work. The identity needs a role on the vault, such as the one that lets it read secrets, and the vault has to be reachable from the app. If either fails, the app may receive the reference text itself instead of the secret, which produces a confusing error, so the portal's reference status is the first place to look. Be clear about the boundary, too. Anyone who can read the running process, or the settings, may be able to reach the value. The strongest answer is to avoid the secret altogether, by letting the identity access storage or databases directly. Next, how do we see what the app is doing?

A running app needs three things from the platform: evidence, a way to be judged healthy, and a way to grow. Evidence first. The log stream shows what each instance prints as it happens, which is perfect for the first look at a problem. Be aware that logging has to be switched on and sent somewhere if you want to keep it. Health checking comes next. You give App Service a path, like slash healthz, and the platform probes it. In the card, instance three keeps failing, so it is taken out of the rotation and the other two serve the traffic. Notice the catch: that rerouting only helps when there is a second instance to take over. For growth there are two directions. Scaling up means a bigger instance. Scaling out means more instances behind the load balancer, and automatic rules for it need a tier that supports them. Finally, keep expectations honest. Scaling is not instant, and adding instances does nothing for a slow database. Capacity helps only when the app itself is the bottleneck. Our last topic in this chapter is releasing new versions safely.

Deploying straight over a live app means a moment of risk. Deployment slots remove most of it. A slot is a live copy of the app with its own hostname. In the table, production runs version twelve and serves every customer, while staging runs version thirteen with a test value for the catalogue address and no traffic. Both slots share the same plan, so they use the same instances. We deploy to staging, test it there, and let the platform warm it up. Then a swap flips the routing: staging becomes production, and the old production code sits in the other slot. If something is wrong, swapping again is the rollback. Settings marked as sticky stay with their slot, which is how staging keeps its own test values. Two cautions. A swap moves code, not database changes, so a schema change needs its own care, which we return to in the delivery chapter. And slots need a qualifying tier. Finally, remember the division of work. Azure patches the operating system and the platform, but your code, your dependencies, your settings and your access remain yours. Next: the network path behind all of this.

Before we can trace our shop's traffic, we need the vocabulary of addresses. An IPv4 address names a network interface and is 32 bits long. Some ranges, such as those starting with 10, are private, which means they are not routed on the public internet, and Azure virtual networks use them. A range is written in CIDR notation. Take ten dot twenty dot one dot zero slash twenty-four. The slash says that the first twenty-four bits identify the network and stay fixed, while the last eight bits vary, so the subnet holds two to the power of eight, which is 256 addresses. A slash sixteen holds 65,536. In the table, notice the last column. Azure reserves five addresses in every subnet, so a slash twenty-four gives 251 you can actually use, and a slash twenty-eight gives only eleven. That matters when you size subnets: count what will live there and add headroom. Finally, an address alone does not say which service you want. A request also names a port and a protocol. Port 443 over TCP is HTTPS, 1433 is SQL Server, and DNS answers on port 53. With that vocabulary, we can build the network itself.

A virtual network, or VNet, is your own private address space inside one Azure region. Nothing in it is reachable from another VNet until you deliberately connect them. In our diagram the network is called vnet-retail, with the range ten dot twenty dot zero dot zero slash sixteen. We slice it into subnets, one per role: a subnet for the web tier, one for data, and one for virtual machines. Why slice it at all? Because most controls attach per subnet. Network security groups and route tables apply to a subnet, and some Azure services, such as gateways and firewalls, insist on a dedicated subnet of their own. Things join a subnet through a network interface. A virtual machine has one, and so does a private endpoint, and each receives a private IP address from the subnet's range. The bottom card is the part people regret skipping. Address planning. If two networks might ever be connected, their ranges must not overlap. Leave room for growth, because resizing a subnet that is in use is awkward. And give each role its own subnet, so rules can match roles. Next, how do packets find their way out?

When a packet leaves a workload, a route decides where it goes next. A route table is a list that maps address prefixes to a next hop. Azure supplies system routes, such as sending traffic within the virtual network directly, and sending everything else to the internet. You can add user-defined routes of your own. Two rules explain nearly every surprise. The most specific prefix wins. And when two routes have the same prefix, a user-defined route beats a system route. In the table, the last row is a user-defined default route that sends internet-bound traffic to a firewall, so it overrides the system one. That raises outbound connectivity, which deserves a clear answer. Virtual machines and apps used to get an implicit outbound address by default, but that default access is being phased out, so do not rely on it. Choose an explicit path. A NAT gateway gives all the outbound traffic from a subnet one stable public address, which partners can allow on their firewalls. A firewall in the path lets you inspect and control egress. When traffic vanishes, ask for the effective routes of the network interface. Now let's control which traffic is allowed at all.

A network security group, or NSG, is Azure's basic packet filter. It is an ordered list of rules, and each rule says a priority, a source, a destination, a port and an action, allow or deny. The lowest priority number is checked first, and the first rule that matches decides. In the table, rule one hundred allows HTTPS from the internet to our web subnet, and rule two hundred denies remote administration from the internet. Below them sit the default rules, which Azure always adds. They allow traffic within the virtual network and deny every other inbound connection. NSGs are stateful, so if an inbound request is allowed, the reply is allowed automatically; you do not write a matching outbound rule. You attach an NSG to a subnet or to a network interface, and the scope matters: a rule on the subnet applies to everything in it. One honest limitation to keep in mind. An NSG sees addresses, ports and protocols. It has no idea who the user is, or whether the request is legitimate. That is the job of other layers, which we meet shortly. First, names.

Almost every connection starts with a name lookup, and many network mysteries are really DNS problems. Public DNS maps a friendly name, shop dot contoso dot com, to a destination. For our app, that is usually a CNAME record that points to the app's default hostname, which then resolves to an address. When you add a custom domain, a TXT record proves that you own it. The lookup in the code card shows the canonical name and the address, and together they tell you which path a client will take. Private DNS is the second half. A private zone answers only for the virtual networks linked to it, and private endpoints depend on it, as we will see in a moment. The consequence is subtle but important: the same name can give different answers inside your network and outside it. That is deliberate, because it lets inside clients reach a private address while everyone else gets the public one. It also means a wrong answer sends traffic down a wrong path. Records also carry a time to live, so changes can take a while to appear. So when something cannot connect, check what the name resolves to before you blame the firewall. Next, securing the connection itself.

Transport Layer Security, or TLS, gives a connection three things: encryption, proof of the server's identity, and protection against tampering. The proof comes from a certificate, and the client checks three things about it: that the name matches the host it asked for, that the certificate chains to an authority it trusts, and that it has not expired. Now a request usually crosses several connections, and TLS is per connection. In the table, the browser connects to a front end, which terminates that connection. The front end then opens a new connection to the app, and the app opens another to the database. Each leg has its own certificate check. A common mistake is to terminate at the edge and leave the back half in plain text, so re-encrypt to the origin. The failures are predictable. A name mismatch means the certificate belongs to another hostname. An expired certificate, or an untrusted chain, breaks the connection outright. Set a minimum TLS version too. So decide where certificates live. Managed certificates renew themselves where they are offered, and others live in Key Vault, but in every case somebody must own renewal. Now, which service should receive the traffic first?

Azure offers several ways to spread requests, and the choice starts with two questions: what protocol layer, and what scope? Load Balancer works at layer four. It sees TCP and UDP connections, not HTTP, which makes it fast and simple, and it works within a single region. Application Gateway works at layer seven. It understands HTTP, so it can route by URL path or host name, handle TLS, and add a web application firewall, but it is also regional. Front Door is also layer seven, but it sits at the global edge. Clients connect to a nearby point of presence, and it can cache content, route to the healthiest of several regions, and apply a web application firewall. The path in the diagram shows one possible design for our shop: the browser looks up the name, DNS points to Front Door, Front Door terminates TLS and applies protections, and the request goes to the App Service origin. These services are not exclusive. A global front door can sit in front of regional gateways. All three probe their backends and stop sending to unhealthy ones, while Traffic Manager routes by DNS alone and never sees the traffic. Choose the least that meets your needs, and justify each extra hop. Next: keeping the origin off the public internet.

Our web app needs to reach its database privately. Three features sound alike, so let's separate them. VNet integration is outbound. It lets the app send traffic into a virtual network, through an integration subnet. It does not make the app itself privately reachable from outside. A private endpoint is the opposite kind of thing: it gives one service instance, here our Azure SQL server, a private IP address inside your subnet. Two cautions. A private endpoint does not by itself switch off the service's public endpoint, so you must disable public access separately. And it grants no permission to the data; you still need the right roles or logins. A service endpoint is an older, simpler idea. It improves the route and lets a service firewall allow your subnet, but the traffic still targets the service's public address. Now the failure in the code card. The app asks for the database name and gets the public address, because the private DNS zone is not linked to this network. With public access disabled, the call fails. The fix is DNS, not another firewall rule. Last, connecting whole networks.

The last networking topic is joining networks together. Virtual network peering connects two VNets over Microsoft's backbone, and from then on they behave like one for routing. But peering is not transitive. If A is peered with B, and B is peered with C, A still cannot reach C. That limitation shapes the hub-spoke design in the diagram. Shared services, such as a central firewall and the gateway to the office, live in a hub network, and each workload gets its own spoke, peered to the hub. Spokes reach each other only if you deliberately route their traffic through the hub. For the way home, there are two kinds of link. A VPN gateway builds an encrypted tunnel across the internet. ExpressRoute is a private circuit from your site to Azure, which avoids the public internet, but private does not mean encrypted: it is not encrypted by default, so add encryption if you need it. Two boundaries to remember. Networks with overlapping address ranges cannot be connected cleanly, which is why we planned addresses early. And a connection only gives you routes. You still need matching security rules at each end. Next, we choose what actually runs our code.

Before comparing products, decide how to decide. Our order API could run in five different places, and the table lists them with what you manage in each. On App Service you manage the code and settings. On a virtual machine you manage the operating system and everything above it. On Container Apps you ship a container image and Azure runs the platform around it. On Kubernetes, through AKS, you manage workloads and nodes. And Azure Functions runs small pieces of event-driven code. The questions on the right pick between them. How much of the stack must you control? Is the load steady, bursty or batch? Can the workload tolerate a cold start, the pause while a new instance spins up? Do you need portability? And, bluntly, who operates this at three in the morning? The rule of thumb is to pick the simplest option that meets the requirements. App Service for a normal web app, Container Apps when you ship containers, virtual machines for special software, and AKS only when you truly need Kubernetes. More control always means more to operate, and the true cost includes patching, upgrades and on-call time. A system can also mix options, and quota and Region availability should be checked first. Let's start at the control end, with virtual machines.

A virtual machine gives you the most control and the most work. It is built from an image, which is the starting operating system, a size that sets the CPU and memory, managed disks for storage, and a network interface. The command in the card creates one with no public IP address, which is deliberate. Lifecycle matters because billing follows it. A running machine bills for compute and for its disks. If you shut it down from inside the operating system, Azure still keeps it allocated, and compute charges continue. Only a deallocated machine stops the compute charge, and its disks keep billing either way. The temporary disk is not durable, so never keep important data there. For access, avoid exposing administration to the internet. Use Azure Bastion or just-in-time access instead, so there is no open remote-login port. Finally, patching is yours. Azure maintains the host, but the guest operating system is your responsibility, so use an update management service rather than logging in and patching by hand. One machine is also a single point of failure, so what keeps a fleet of them healthy?

A virtual machine scale set manages many identical machines as one unit. You describe a model, once, and the scale set creates instances from it. In the diagram, three instances run in three different zones, which protects against the loss of a datacenter. It also watches health. Instance two is failing its check, so the scale set replaces it rather than leaving it in the pool. Autoscale rules can add or remove instances based on a metric such as CPU or queue length. Note the consequence: for instances to be replaceable, they must be stateless, because a new instance will not have the old one's local data. Updates can roll through in batches, as long as you keep spare capacity. Now the limits, which people often misunderstand. Quota is a ceiling on what you are allowed to use. It is not capacity set aside for you. When you ask for more instances, a particular size in a particular zone may simply not be available at that moment. So plan for fallback sizes, and if your workload truly needs guaranteed capacity, look at reserving it. Next, a different packaging: the container image.

Containers package an application and its dependencies into one portable image. The Dockerfile in the card says how: start from a slim Python base image, install the requirements, copy in the code, and define the command. The result runs the same way on a laptop, in Container Apps or on Kubernetes. Images live in a registry, and Azure Container Registry is the Azure one. Look at the two cards inside it. A tag, like one dot four dot two, is a friendly label, but a tag can be moved to point at different content later. A digest is an identifier of the exact content, and it can never change, so pinning by digest is how you know precisely what is running. The registry is also where trust is decided. Allow only a few identities to push images. Scan them, and sign them if your policy requires it, before they run. Let workloads pull using a managed identity with a pull-only role, never a shared password. Keep images small, run as a non-root user, and never bake secrets in. And remember base images age, so rebuild regularly to pick up patches. With an image in a registry, where do we run it?

Azure Container Apps runs containers without making you operate a Kubernetes cluster. You create an environment, which provides shared networking and logging, and then deploy apps into it. The command in the card deploys our order API image, enables external ingress on port 8000, and lets the app run between zero and five replicas. Each time you change the app's definition, Container Apps creates a revision. A revision is an immutable snapshot, so you can run two at once and split traffic between them: in the diagram, eighty percent goes to revision one and twenty percent to revision two, which is a canary release you can roll back by shifting the split. Jobs are the other workload shape. A job runs to completion, such as a nightly export, instead of waiting for requests. It suits stateless APIs, workers and event processors, and it does not expose the Kubernetes API. Scaling follows rules: concurrent HTTP requests, the length of a queue, or a schedule. Scale to zero is attractive because an idle app costs very little, but the price is a cold start when the first request arrives. If your latency target cannot absorb that, keep at least one replica running. And when containers are not enough?

Azure Kubernetes Service gives you Kubernetes without installing it yourself. Kubernetes is an orchestrator: you declare what you want, such as three replicas of the order API, and it keeps reality matching that declaration. The manifest in the card is exactly that declaration. In an AKS cluster, Azure runs the control plane, the part that makes the decisions. But the rest is still yours. You choose and size the node pools, which are virtual machines, and you upgrade them. You write and maintain the manifests, health probes and resource limits for the workloads. You add and operate the pieces around the cluster, such as ingress, policy and monitoring. You also own cluster security, such as network policy and pod identity. And you keep the Kubernetes version moving forward, because versions go out of support. So when is it worth it? When you need Kubernetes itself, its API, its ecosystem, or its portability across environments, and when you have a team who can operate it. If you only need to run containers, Container Apps is simpler. How do all these options scale, and what goes wrong when they do?

The last topic in this chapter ties the options together: scaling is never instant. Follow the timeline. Load rises and latency climbs. A metric must cross a threshold, usually for a window of time, before a rule fires. Then a new instance has to start: pull the image, boot, and warm up. Only then does it take traffic. And sometimes the capacity you ask for is late, or not available at all. That delay is why the choice of signal matters. A signal that leads the problem, like the length of a queue, helps more than one that lags, like CPU after users are already waiting. Two properties make replacement safe. First, instances must be stateless. In the diagram, a session held in an instance's memory is lost when that instance is replaced, while a session in a shared store survives. Second, shutdown must be graceful. When Azure scales in, it sends a termination signal. The handler in the card finishes in-flight work and exits, instead of cutting requests mid-way. Load test the rule before launch, because an untested scaling rule is a guess. Now that compute can be replaced at will, where does the data that must survive live?

The last chapter ended with a promise: compute can be replaced at will, so durable data needs a proper home. Azure storage comes in three shapes, and each is defined by the interface your software uses. Object storage holds whole objects, such as images and documents, which you read and write over HTTPS in a flat namespace. That is Blob Storage, and it is the one we will spend most time on. File storage is a shared drive. Many clients mount the same share over SMB or NFS and see the same files, which is what Azure Files provides. Block storage is a disk. A virtual machine formats it and mounts it, and gets low-latency access for one machine, which is what managed disks provide. The table maps each to our shop. Product images are objects, shared configuration is a file share, and database data files sit on block disks. Now the persistence boundary in the bottom card. Local disk and memory vanish when an instance is replaced. If it must survive, it belongs in a storage service. For files an app reads and writes by name, prefer object storage. Let's open up the most common one.

Blob Storage has a three-level structure. At the top is the storage account, which is the namespace and the unit you configure and pay for. Its name is globally unique, three to twenty-four lowercase letters and digits, and it appears in every URL, so it is worth planning. Inside the account are containers, which group blobs, and inside containers are the blobs themselves, the actual objects. The command in the card uploads a receipt file into a container called receipts, using the signed-in identity rather than a key. Every blob has a URL that follows the structure: the account, then the container, then the blob name. You can upload, download, list, copy and delete, and the operations are the same whether you use the CLI, an SDK or plain HTTPS. Two choices at creation matter. The account type and redundancy decide which features you get, and the region cannot be changed later. Finally, think about the access path. By default the account has a public endpoint. You can instead reach it through a private endpoint inside your network, as we saw in the networking chapter. Who is allowed to read and write is the next question.

We met data roles in the identity chapter, and now we can compare all the ways to authorise a blob request. From narrow to broad, the first is a managed identity with a data role. The app proves who it is, the role says what it may do, and there is no secret to store, leak or rotate. That should be the default. Next is a shared access signature, or SAS. A SAS is a signed URL that carries a permission, a scope and an expiry. In the card, this one gives read-only access to a single blob until a specific time. A SAS made with Entra credentials is called a user delegation SAS, and is preferable to one signed with the account key. Be clear about the risk: whoever holds the URL can use it until it expires, and you cannot see who they passed it to. The broadest option is the account key, which gives full access to everything in the account and bypasses roles entirely. Where you can, disable shared-key access. In practice: narrowest scope, shortest time, and use a short-lived SAS only for one-off sharing. Next, what happens when two writers collide.

Suppose two parts of our shop update the same receipt at the same time. Blob Storage is strongly consistent, which means once a write succeeds, the next read sees it. But that guarantee is per blob. There are no transactions across several blobs, so two related blobs can never be updated atomically. For one blob, the tool for concurrent writers is the ETag. Every blob has an ETag that changes whenever it is written. The table shows the pattern. Both writers read the blob and get version one. Writer A writes first, with an If-Match header naming version one, and it succeeds, so the blob becomes version two. Writer B then writes with the same If-Match header. The condition no longer holds, and the service answers 412, precondition failed, instead of silently overwriting A's change. B should re-read and retry. A lease is the heavier alternative: a timed, exclusive lock, which suits short critical sections, with renewal. With no condition, the last writer simply wins, and a conditional create can use if-none-match with a star. Design accordingly. Expect to retry after a 412, and never assume two blobs change together. Next, protecting data from the changes we make ourselves.

Data has a life, and Azure gives you controls for each stage. First, access tiers. Hot is for frequently used data. Cool, cold and archive are progressively cheaper to store but more expensive to read, and archive is offline, so reading it means rehydrating it, which can take hours. Rather than moving blobs by hand, a lifecycle rule does it by age. The card moves anything under receipts to cool after thirty days and to archive after one hundred and eighty. Second, protection against our own mistakes. The table follows a blob over four days. Versioning keeps the old content when it is overwritten, and soft delete keeps a deleted blob for a retention period, so on day three we can undelete it. Be honest about what that covers. Both protect against mistakes. A person with enough permission can still remove versions and soft-deleted data. For stronger guarantees, immutable storage stores data in a write-once, read-many way, so it cannot be changed or deleted until the retention period ends. Remember that versions and soft-deleted data still cost money. Now, the other storage shapes.

Two other storage services complete the picture. Azure Files is a managed file share. Clients mount it over SMB or NFS, and many of them can use it at once, which is what the three clients in the diagram do. It is a good fit for shared configuration, or for moving an old file server to the cloud without rewriting it. A managed disk is different. It is block storage, and it is normally attached to one virtual machine at a time, which formats it and mounts it like a local drive. Disks come in types that trade cost for performance, and a disk is persistent, so it outlives the machine it was attached to. Look at the lifecycle in the bottom card. You create a disk, attach it, snapshot it to capture a point in time, and eventually delete it. The last step is the one people forget, because a detached disk still exists and still bills, as in our cost ledger from the first chapter. To choose, ask about sharing. Many clients with one namespace point to Files. One machine that needs low latency points to a disk. Finally, how many copies, and where?

We finish the chapter with the most misunderstood word in storage: redundancy. Redundancy keeps extra copies of your data. Locally redundant storage keeps three copies inside one datacentre. Zone-redundant storage keeps three copies across zones. Geo-redundant options add a further copy in another region, and that copy is made asynchronously, so a regional failover can lose the most recent writes. Geo-replication therefore does not mean zero data loss. Now the key distinction, drawn in the bottom card. Replication protects against hardware and site loss. But a replica faithfully copies a deletion, an overwrite or a corruption, because it is just another copy. Each threat needs its own control. Mistakes call for versioning and soft delete. Corruption or an attacker calls for immutable or isolated backups. And for any of them, the claim that data is recoverable is only as good as a tested restore. So when someone says the data is safe because it is geo-redundant, ask what happens after someone deletes it. With persistence settled, we can organise transactional data: databases.

A database choice is a choice about how your data will be used, so start with questions, not products. The table lists four models and what each is strong at, with an example from our shop. A relational database stores tables and supports joins and transactions, which suits orders and stock. A document database stores one JSON item per record, so a read fetches everything about one thing, which suits a product catalogue. A key-value cache keeps hot data in memory for very fast reads. And object storage holds large files. The questions on the right decide between them. What are the queries: simple lookups, joins across tables, or scans? What must be atomic, meaning it either all happens or none of it does? Money and stock usually must be. How fast must it be and how big will it grow? And who owns the data? That last one matters more than it sounds: each piece of data should have one owning service and one home, even if the system uses several models overall. In our shop that means orders in a relational database and the catalogue as documents, sized for growth. Let's start with the relational family on Azure.

Microsoft offers the SQL Server engine in three forms on Azure, ordered by how much you manage. Azure SQL Database is a fully managed database. Azure patches the engine, takes backups and provides availability, and you manage the schema and the queries. It is the natural home for a new cloud application, and new features usually arrive there first. SQL Managed Instance is a managed instance with very high compatibility with on-premises SQL Server, including features that work at the instance level. It suits migrations of existing applications, and it lives inside your virtual network. SQL Server on a virtual machine hands you full control of the operating system and the engine, and with it responsibility for patching, backups and high availability. The decision rule is simple: prefer the most managed option that is compatible with what the application needs, and move toward more control only for a named requirement, such as a feature the managed options do not offer. You pay for compute and storage, and reserving capacity can lower the price. The table shows the trade. The same selection thinking applies to open-source engines.

Not every application is built for SQL Server, and Azure treats PostgreSQL as a first-class managed service. Azure Database for PostgreSQL runs the open-source engine, with Azure operating the servers, backups and patching. You choose it for the PostgreSQL ecosystem: the extensions, the tooling, and the portability of an engine that runs anywhere. There is also a managed MySQL service. How should you choose between all of these? Let the application lead. If the code uses T-SQL and SQL Server features, look at Azure SQL. If it depends on PostgreSQL extensions, use PostgreSQL. Changing engines just for taste means schema and code changes, not just moving data. The table on the screen turns that into a lookup. The bottom card lists questions that apply to every managed relational service, and they are worth asking each time. Which versions are supported, and when do they retire? What high availability options exist, within a zone or across regions? How long are backups kept and how does restore work? And how do you reach the service privately? With the choice made, how does the application use it correctly?

Choosing a database is only half the job. Using it correctly is the other half. The SQL in the card places one order as a single transaction. It inserts the order, inserts its line item, and reduces the stock, and then commits. A transaction is all or nothing: if any step fails, none of them take effect. The condition on the stock update protects against selling something we do not have. Now look at the second table, which is a hypothetical trace of a classic failure. Each app instance keeps a pool of connections. With three instances and a pool of twenty, that is sixty connections, comfortably under the server's limit. Scale out to twelve instances and the same setting means two hundred and forty, and the server starts refusing connections. So the pool size must be chosen with scale-out in mind. For authentication, prefer Entra authentication with a managed identity over a password. Finally, retries. Transient errors happen, so retry them with backoff, but retry the whole transaction, never half of one, and make the operation idempotent, so a repeat does no harm. Next: availability and the difference between a replica and a backup.

Three tools get confused because they all involve extra copies, but each answers a different question. High availability keeps the database running when a node or even a whole zone fails. It is about continuity. It does not protect you from someone running a bad update, because the bad update is replicated too. A read replica is a copy that serves reads, which helps when the primary is overwhelmed by queries. But replicas are asynchronous, so a replica can be a little behind. The table traces the effect. At zero seconds the price is set to twenty on the primary. At four tenths of a second a shopper reads from the replica and still sees eighteen. By one point two seconds it catches up. That is fine for a catalogue page and wrong for checking out. Reads that must be fresh go to the primary. Backups answer the third question: how do I get back to before the mistake? Point-in-time restore brings back an earlier state, usually into a new database, so practise it, and time it against your recovery target. A replica is not a backup. Every managed service differs in its retention and behaviour, so check yours. Now a different model: Cosmos DB.

Cosmos DB is a globally distributed document database, and we will use its NoSQL API as our concrete example. A container holds JSON items, and every item carries a value for the partition key. Items sharing a key value form a logical partition, and Azure spreads partitions across physical machines. So the partition key is the most important design choice you will make. The card shows an order item that uses the customer identifier as its key. The table compares candidates. The customer identifier has many values, spread evenly, so it is a good key. The order date is a poor key, because today's orders all share one value, so all the writes land on one partition. A country is skewed, because a few big countries dominate. Throughput is measured in request units per second and is divided across partitions. That is why a hot partition is throttled even while the container's total capacity sits idle. By default Cosmos DB indexes every property, which makes queries flexible but costs on writes, so tune the indexing policy once you know your queries. The next question is how consistent reads need to be.

A distributed database makes you choose how fresh a read must be, and Cosmos DB offers five consistency levels. Strong guarantees that a read sees the latest write, at the highest latency. Eventual might return any older state, at the lowest cost. Between them sit bounded staleness, session, and consistent prefix. Session is the default, and it guarantees that a client sees its own writes, which fits most applications. The trade-off is straightforward: stronger consistency costs latency, and across regions it also costs availability. Now the scope of atomic work, which people often overestimate. A transactional batch is atomic, but only within one logical partition. There is no transaction across partitions, so a design that needs cross-partition atomicity needs another approach. For concurrent writers, use the item's ETag, just as we did with blobs. Finally, if you accept writes in several regions, two regions can modify the same item at once, and you need a conflict-resolution policy. Choose these settings per workload rather than once for everything. Our last data topic is the cache that sits in front of it all.

A cache puts hot data in fast memory in front of the database. The most common pattern is cache-aside, shown in the card. Look in the cache first. If the value is missing, read it from the database, store it in the cache with a time to live, and return it. The cost of that speed is staleness. The table runs a timeline. A price of eighteen is cached, and at sixty seconds the real price changes to twenty. Until the entry expires at three hundred seconds, shoppers still see eighteen. So decide, for each kind of data, how stale is acceptable, and invalidate explicitly when it is not. A word on products. Azure Managed Redis is the current choice for new caches, while Azure Cache for Redis is on a retirement path, so treat it as a migration context and verify the dates. The same mindset applies when moving to a new database. Copy the bulk, then keep syncing changes. Reconcile counts and checksums, so you can prove nothing was lost. And plan the way back before you cut over, because rollback is hardest after the fact. With data in place, we can connect the pieces with APIs and messages.

When other teams or partners call your API, you do not want every backend to reinvent authentication, rate limits and versioning. API Management is a gateway that sits in front of the backends and does those jobs once. In the diagram a partner app calls slash orders. The gateway publishes the contract, usually an OpenAPI definition, so callers know what to expect. It authenticates the caller before the backend sees the request, and it applies policies: transforming a message, caching a response, logging the call. The card shows a trimmed policy. It validates the bearer token against Entra, rejecting a bad one with a 401, and it limits each caller to a hundred calls per minute. It can also expose versions, so old clients keep working. Because the rules live in one place, backends stay simple and can change behind a stable address. Be realistic about the limits. A gateway does not fix a slow backend. You should keep the backend private so that it can only be reached through the gateway. And decisions about which data a given caller may see still belong in the backend. Behind the gateway, much of our logic can run as small functions.

Azure Functions lets you run small pieces of code in response to events, without managing servers. Every function has three parts. The trigger is what starts it: a message arriving on a queue, a timer, an HTTP request. A function has exactly one trigger, chosen from HTTP, timer, queue, Service Bus, Event Hubs, Event Grid and more. The handler is your code, which here is plain Python that receives the trigger's data. And bindings are declarative connections for inputs and outputs. In the card, the decorators say this function runs when a message arrives on the orders queue, and that it writes its result to a second queue called fulfil. The runtime does the reading and writing, so the handler stays short. Notice the connection setting is a name that points to an app setting, so no secret sits in the code. Now the boundaries, which shape how you write handlers. There is a time limit, and it depends on the hosting plan. And there is no local state, because instances are added and removed as load changes, so anything that must last belongs in a store. Which hosting plan to choose is next.

A function's hosting plan decides how it scales, what networking it can use, and how it behaves when idle. For a new serverless app, evaluate Flex Consumption first where it is available. It scales per function, can scale to zero, and supports virtual network integration. The older Consumption plan also scales to zero, but check its current status and limits before you start something new on it. Premium keeps pre-warmed instances, which gives steadier latency. Dedicated runs your functions on an App Service plan you already own. Whichever you choose, use a managed identity to reach storage and queues, and remember that networking options vary by plan. Concurrency matters too: one instance can run many invocations at once, so tune it to what your dependencies can take. Now the most overlooked point, shown in the card: who retries? It depends on the trigger. A queue trigger relies on the queue to redeliver and eventually parks poison messages. Service Bus uses locks, retries and dead-lettering. For an HTTP trigger, the caller retries. A timer simply runs again at the next time. Never assume a retry exists. Next, the services that carry the messages.

Azure has more than one queue, and the right one depends on the delivery rules you need. Queue Storage is simple and inexpensive, with very large capacity. The trade is that it gives no ordering guarantee, and handling poison messages is something you build yourself. Service Bus is the full messaging service. Sessions give you ordered delivery for messages that share a key. A dead-letter queue is built in, so messages that keep failing are parked rather than lost. Duplicate detection is available as an option. Topics and subscriptions let many subscribers each receive a copy of a message, and transactions can group operations. The table lines the capabilities up. How do you choose? Start with the delivery rules you need, not the price. If you only need to hand work from one component to another, and simple is enough, Queue Storage is a good fit. If you need ordering, dead-lettering, publish and subscribe, or transactions, use Service Bus. Both deliver at least once, and payload size limits differ, so check them. And be careful with one claim: neither service on its own gives you exactly-once business effects. We will come back to that. First, how Service Bus settles messages.

Service Bus delivers messages in peek-lock mode. When your code receives a message, the service locks it, which hides it from other receivers, and waits for you to settle it. You can complete it, meaning it is done and can be removed. You can abandon it, releasing it for another try. You can dead-letter it, parking it for inspection. Or you can defer it, to fetch later by its number. After a maximum number of delivery attempts, the service dead-letters the message for you. Now the failure the table traces, which catches many teams. The lock lasts sixty seconds, but our database work takes seventy-five. At forty seconds the update succeeds. At sixty the lock expires, and the message becomes visible again. At seventy-five our Complete call fails because the lock is lost, and a second delivery happens. The work was done twice. Sessions keep messages ordered per key, and duplicate detection drops repeated sends within a window, but neither makes your handler safe against a redelivery. Next, a different kind of messaging: events.

Not everything is a command. Sometimes a system just wants to announce that something happened. That is an event, and Azure Event Grid distributes events from sources to subscribers. In our diagram, the storage account emits an event whenever a blob is created. The card shows it trimmed: its type, a subject naming the blob, and a time. Event Grid does not decide what to do about it. Subscriptions do. Each subscription filters the events it cares about and routes them to a handler, which might be a function that processes the receipt, a queue that buffers the work, or a webhook that notifies a partner. Delivery is at least once. If a handler is down, Event Grid retries with backoff, and it can send events that never delivered to a dead-letter store. That means handlers must tolerate duplicates. Event Grid fits notification and reaction well, such as processing a file as soon as it lands. It is not designed for high-volume continuous streams, and that is the job of Event Hubs, which is next.

When events arrive as a continuous, high-volume stream, such as every click or every order change, Event Hubs is the service built for it. An event hub is a partitioned log. Events are appended to partitions, and order is guaranteed only within a partition, never across them. If events about the same order must stay in order, send them with the same partition key, which routes them to the same partition. Consumers read through consumer groups. Each group reads the whole stream independently, so an analytics job and an alerting job can share one hub without interfering. The table shows why. Each group keeps its own checkpoint, a record of how far it has read. After a restart it resumes from that point, which also means some events can be processed again. Lag is simply the newest offset minus the checkpoint. The analytics group is a hundred events behind, while alerts are almost current. A lagging consumer needs more consumers, up to the number of partitions, or faster processing. With streams understood, how do we coordinate multi-step work?

A real order touches several services: reserve stock, take payment, create a shipment. Any step can fail, and you cannot roll back a payment the way a database rolls back a transaction. The answer is an orchestration with compensation. Look at the orchestrator in the card. It reserves stock, then charges payment. If the charge throws an exception, the orchestrator runs a compensating activity that releases the stock, and then re-raises. Durable Functions provides this. The orchestrator coordinates the work, while each activity does one real step. There is a rule that surprises people: an orchestrator is replayed from its history each time it resumes, so its code must be deterministic. It must not read the clock, generate random numbers, or call services directly. Those side effects belong in activities. Logic Apps is the other tool. You build workflows visually, with a large library of connectors, which suits integration with other systems. Test the failure paths, not only the happy one. Choose Durable Functions when you want code, tests and source control, and Logic Apps when connectors and a visual flow matter more. The final section ties everything together: retries and duplicates.

Everything in this chapter delivers at least once, which means any handler can run twice. Duplicate detection, ordered sessions and checkpoints all reduce repeats, but none of them can promise that your business effect happens exactly once. The only reliable defence is to make the effect itself idempotent, meaning a repeat does no harm. The card shows one way: a fulfilments table with the order identifier as its primary key. The first delivery inserts the key and ships the parcel. A duplicate delivery hits a key violation, so the handler skips the shipping and acknowledges the message. The unique key, in the same database as the effect, is what makes the guard reliable. Around that, keep the pipeline healthy. Retry transient faults with backoff, and cap the attempts. A message that keeps failing is a poison message, so park it for a human rather than letting it block the queue forever. And let a slow consumer push back on the producer, so that backlog cannot grow without limit. That completes our application plumbing. Now, how do operational changes feed analysis and reporting?

So far we have built the operational side of our shop: an application that takes orders and stores them. Now the business asks different questions. Which products sold best last quarter? What was revenue by region each week? Did last month's numbers change? Those are analytical questions, and the table shows how they differ from the operational ones. An operational system serves the application: fetch one order by key, write a small change, answer immediately, and hold only the current state. An analytical system serves people and reports. It scans and aggregates over a lot of rows, keeps years of history, and can often tolerate results that are minutes or even a day old. You might wonder why not simply run reports on the operational database. There are three reasons. Heavy queries slow the application down. Operational schemas, which are normalised for writes, are awkward to analyse. And history is overwritten in place, so last month's value is gone. The usual answer is to copy data out, shape it for analysis, and serve it from a separate system. First, how the data gets there.

How does data get from the operational database into analytics? The table lists four methods. A full load copies everything each time. It is simple, but gets expensive as the data grows. A watermark approach copies only the rows changed since the last run, like the query in the card, which uses a half-open window so no boundary row is counted twice or skipped. Its weakness is that it misses hard deletes, and any change that does not update the timestamp. Change data capture reads the source's change log, so it sees inserts, updates and deletes accurately, at the cost of more setup and sensitivity to schema changes. An event stream consumes changes as they happen, and brings duplicates and ordering questions of its own. Whichever you choose, agree a source contract with the owner of the data: which columns, what they mean, and how changes will be announced, because a silent schema change breaks the pipeline. And reconcile. Compare row counts and totals with the source, so you can show the numbers match. A pipeline that ran successfully is not proof that it ran correctly. Next, where does the data land?

Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 is Blob Storage with a hierarchical namespace, which gives real folders. The layout matters. The paths in the card use three zones: raw, for data exactly as received; curated, for cleaned data; and serving, for what consumers read. Folders are partitioned by a field that queries commonly filter on, here a date. A query for one day then reads one folder and skips the rest, which is called partition pruning. For format, prefer Parquet. It is columnar and compressed, so analytical queries read less. CSV is easy to inspect but large and untyped. Many tiny files slow queries, so compact them. Now access, where people often assume both a role and an ACL are always required. It depends on how the caller authenticates. With an Entra identity, Azure checks the RBAC data roles first. If a role allows the request, the ACLs are not evaluated. Only if RBAC does not allow it are the ACLs checked. A shared key or SAS token bypasses ACLs altogether. In practice, grant access to groups, at the narrowest folder that works. Now let's orchestrate the movement of data.

Moving data reliably needs orchestration, and Azure Data Factory is the service we will use as the concrete example. A pipeline is a chain of activities started by a trigger, such as a nightly schedule. The card shows a trimmed Copy activity, which reads from a SQL dataset and writes Parquet to the lake. The diagram shows the whole nightly pipeline. Copy the orders to the raw zone, transform them into the curated zone, load a summary table, and alert somebody if any step fails. Note the division of labour: Data Factory orchestrates and moves data, while other engines do heavier computation. A few habits make pipelines dependable. Use parameters, so the same pipeline works in development and production. Add alerts, with a named person who owns them. And configure retries for transient faults. You pay for activity runs and data movement, so avoid chatty pipelines. Then there is governance, which is a separate job from running the pipeline. A catalogue records what data exists, what it means and who owns it. Lineage shows where a number came from. Without them, the lake becomes a swamp. Which analytics platform sits on top is the next choice.

Three Microsoft analytics platforms are easy to confuse, and the difference is mainly in the control surface. Azure Synapse Analytics is a set of Azure resources: SQL engines, Spark and pipelines. You govern it the way you govern other Azure resources, through subscriptions, resource groups and role assignments. Azure Databricks is also an Azure resource, hosting a Spark-based lakehouse, with its own workspace and its own catalogue. It deserves a specialist treatment of its own, so we treat it as a companion subject. Microsoft Fabric is different in kind. It is a software-as-a-service platform built around OneLake. You manage it through tenant settings, workspaces and capacities, not through resource groups. It even has its own Data Factory experience, which we should compare separately from the Azure one. So when you evaluate a platform, ask where the bill and the access are managed. And be aware that product direction in this area changes quickly, so verify current guidance rather than trusting a table. Finally, what if the data cannot wait for a nightly run?

Sometimes a nightly batch is too slow, and we need results from a stream. Streaming brings a distinction batch hides: event time versus processing time. Event time is when something happened. Processing time is when the system received it. They can differ by minutes, because of network delays or retries. The Stream Analytics query in the card counts orders by product in five-minute tumbling windows, grouping events into fixed periods by their order time. Now suppose an order placed at ten oh four arrives at ten oh seven. The table shows the choice. If you allow no lateness, the window closes at ten oh five and the late event is dropped or adjusted, but the result is available on time. If you allow three minutes of lateness, the event is counted, but every result waits until ten oh eight. So lateness trades accuracy against freshness. Add two more pressures: replays and retries can duplicate events, and an always-on streaming job costs money all day. So decide what matters. A fast, approximate answer, or a late, accurate one? And if a day-old answer is fine, use batch. With analytics in place, how do we reproduce all this infrastructure reliably?

So far we created resources by typing commands. That works for a first request, but it does not scale, and it leaves no record of what should exist. Infrastructure as code solves that, and on Azure the native language is Bicep. Bicep is declarative: you describe the end state you want, and Azure works out the steps. That makes running it twice safe. Bicep compiles to an ARM template, the JSON that Azure Resource Manager understands, but you review and edit the Bicep, which is far more readable. Look at the resource line in the card. The type names the resource provider and the kind, here a server farm, which is the App Service plan from chapter three. After the at sign comes the API version, and that matters. It fixes the shape of the resource's properties, so a newer version can bring new properties, and you should pin the version deliberately. A final point about ownership. Once a resource is declared in a file under source control, that file owns it. A manual change in the portal is drift, and it will be flagged or overwritten at the next deployment. Next, structuring larger deployments.

A real deployment has many resources, so Bicep gives you ways to organise them. A module is a Bicep file that you call with parameters, from another file. In the card, the main file declares the plan, then calls a web module, and passes it the plan's identifier. Modules let you create one per unit of ownership, such as a web tier, and reuse it across environments. That identifier is also a reference, and references do something valuable. Because the web module uses the plan's identifier, Azure Resource Manager knows the plan must be deployed first. You rarely write dependencies by hand. Resources with no relationship are deployed in parallel. The last concept is scope. Most workloads deploy at the resource group scope. Creating resource groups themselves, and subscription-level policy, deploys at the subscription scope. A management group scope covers wide policy, and the tenant scope is rare and highly privileged. Keep modules small, and share them through a versioned registry. As with role assignments, choose the smallest scope that works. Now, how do the same files serve development and production?

One template should serve every environment, so the parts that differ go into parameters. A parameter file, like the one in the card, sets the app name and the tier for development. Production gets its own file with its own values. Secrets need extra care, and here is the rule. A secret is never written into a template or a parameter file. The card shows the alternative: the password parameter is fetched from Key Vault at deployment time, by reference, and the parameter is marked secure. The table sums up where each kind of value belongs. Names and sizes go in the parameter file. A secret goes in Key Vault, and is referenced. An identifier that other deployments need can be an output. Outputs deserve caution, because deployment logs print them. So never output a secret, and treat build logs as if they were public. Make it part of review. Search the diff for keys and tokens, and check what the outputs reveal. With a template written, how do we know what a change will do before we run it?

Before changing production, you want to see what a deployment will do. What-if gives you that preview. The card shows a trimmed example. A tilde means a resource will be modified, here turning always-on to true on the web app. A plus means a resource will be created, such as an Application Insights component. And a minus means a deletion. Review it before anyone approves the change. That minus line connects to deployment modes. The default, incremental mode, only adds and updates. It never deletes resources that the template omits. Complete mode is different, and can delete anything not in the template, so use it deliberately, with a review, or with a mechanism built for managing deletions. What-if also surfaces drift. A change made by hand in the portal is compared with the file, and the next deployment may revert it. Now the honest limits. A clean what-if cannot promise the deployment will succeed, because quota, name conflicts and policy can still fail it. And it may not show runtime consequences, such as an app restarting. It is a review aid, not a guarantee. Next: who runs the deployment?

Someone, or something, has to run these deployments, and giving a pipeline a stored client secret is a liability. If it leaks, an attacker can deploy as you, and it must be rotated forever. Workload identity federation removes the secret. Look at the trust relationship in the diagram. The CI provider, here GitHub, issues a short-lived token to the running job. Entra has a federated credential that trusts tokens from one specific repository and environment. The pipeline exchanges the token for an Azure access token for a particular identity, and nothing long-lived is ever stored. The workflow in the card shows how little it needs: permission to request the token, and a login step with three identifiers, none of which is a secret. Apply least privilege on top. Use one deployment identity per environment, and give each a role only on its own resource group, so the development identity cannot touch production.
