Run what-if on the pull request, and deploy only after merge and approval. And check that the federated credential names the exact subject, not a wildcard. Deploying infrastructure is one thing, but releasing software safely has its own risks.

Releasing software is riskier than deploying infrastructure, because software changes have to coexist with state. Start with what a rollback does. A slot swap or a traffic shift reverts the application code. It does not revert the database. If version thirteen has already changed the schema, putting version twelve back in front of it may fail. The answer is to make schema changes in steps, called expand and contract. The table shows renaming a column. First, expand: add the new column and keep the old one, so version twelve still works. Second, release version thirteen, which uses both columns, and fill the new one. Third, verify that only version thirteen is running. Only then, in the fourth step, contract: drop the old column. After that last step, an application rollback no longer restores the old behaviour, because the old column is gone. Alongside this, use canaries. Send a small percentage of traffic to the new version first and watch errors and latency before widening it. Feature flags help too, because they separate deploying code from releasing it. The rule behind it all is that every schema change must work with two adjacent application versions. Last, how a build moves between environments.

The last delivery principle is to build once and promote. The pipeline builds the application a single time and records the result as an artefact, with an image digest and the commit it came from. That same artefact goes to development, then to test, then to production, with only the parameters changing. Production waits for an approval. Because you never rebuild for production, what you tested is what you ship. Alongside that, record provenance: who built what, from which commit, and the digest of what is running, so you can answer the question what is in production right now. Finally, a word on tools. Bicep is Azure-only and Azure tracks the state of your deployments, so there is no state file to protect. Terraform covers many providers, and uses a state file that you must secure and back up. Neither is better in the abstract. Choose for your team's skills and scope, and if you use both, split responsibilities clearly so they do not fight over the same resources. The delivery is now reproducible. Next, how do we see and recover what we have built?

When something goes wrong in production, you need evidence, and Azure Monitor deals with three kinds. Metrics are numbers over time, such as request rate and CPU. They are cheap, they aggregate well, and they suit alerts, because they answer the question: is it healthy? Logs record a single event with full detail, answering: what happened? Write them structured, as fields rather than free text, like the card, so that you can query them. And traces follow one request across several services, answering: where did the time go? What ties the three together is a correlation identifier. In the diagram, the request, the dependency call and the log line all carry the same operation identifier, so from a slow request you can find the exact failed call to the catalogue and the error it logged. Without that identifier, you are guessing which log line belongs to which request. One more decision belongs here: retention. Keeping every signal forever costs real money, so decide how long each one remains useful. Next, how to ask questions of all this data.

Azure Monitor is the umbrella service for metrics, logs and alerts. Application Insights collects telemetry from your application, such as requests and exceptions, and a Log Analytics workspace stores it and lets you query it. The query language is KQL, and the card shows a first useful query. You start from a table, here the requests table. A where line filters to the last hour. A summarize line aggregates, producing a count and the ninety-fifth percentile of duration, grouped by the request name, and the order by line sorts the slowest first. The table shows the output we would expect from a small synthetic dataset. One row per request name. The order endpoint has two hundred and twelve calls with a ninety-fifth percentile of nineteen hundred milliseconds, which stands out, while the health check is fast. A percentile deserves a note: ninety-fifth percentile means ninety-five percent of calls were faster than that value, which tells you more about the slow tail than an average does. A good habit is to limit the time range first, because it makes queries faster and cheaper. Next, getting the right data collected.

A common surprise during an investigation is discovering the data you need was never kept. The table is the antidote. Platform metrics are collected automatically, but only for a limited time. The Activity Log records control-plane events across the subscription, and is kept briefly. Resource logs, the detailed logs from services such as storage or databases, are not collected at all until you configure a diagnostic setting. And application telemetry needs an SDK or an agent. In short, telemetry being available is not the same as it being collected and retained. A diagnostic setting routes a resource's logs to a destination: a Log Analytics workspace if you want to query and alert, a storage account for cheap long retention, or Event Hubs to stream to another system. Set them per resource, and ideally enforce them with policy so nothing is missed. The Activity Log entry in the card is audit evidence. It shows who made a role assignment, and when. But it records management actions, not data reads. Before an audit, check the scope and the retention actually match the question. Now, turning signals into promises and alerts.

Telemetry is only useful if it leads to action. Start with an objective. An indicator is what you measure, such as the share of requests that succeed. The objective is the target. In the table, ninety-nine point nine percent over thirty days. The part you are allowed to miss is the error budget. A thirty-day month has forty-three thousand two hundred minutes, so a one tenth of a percent budget is about forty-three minutes. Those numbers are illustrative, and the real targets belong to the owning team and the business. Alerts should follow the objective. Alert on symptoms that users feel, and fire when the budget is burning fast, rather than paging someone for every possible cause. Too many alerts become noise, and noise gets ignored. When an alert fires, an action group decides who and what is told, whether people, a chat channel, or an automated system. A runbook holds the first safe steps, so the person paged does not have to invent them. And someone must own the alert, by name. Finally, review and tune alerts after every incident. Next, the secrets and keys that these systems depend on.

Key Vault stores secrets, encryption keys and certificates, with access controlled by role assignments and every access logged. The hard part is not storing a secret, it is changing one without breaking things. Look at the timeline in the table. We rotate a database password. At step one the database now rejects the old value. At step two the app still holds the old secret, so logins fail. At step three the vault has the new secret, but the app has not re-read it. Only at step four, when the app picks up the vault's new value, does it recover. The lesson is to plan the order, and to make sure consumers re-read the secret instead of caching it forever. Rotation is a practised procedure, not an emergency improvisation. Now see that the vault itself becomes a dependency. If it is unreachable when an app starts, the app may not start. And if you use a customer-managed encryption key, disabling that key makes the encrypted data unreadable, by design. So turn on soft delete and purge protection, and monitor access and failures. Beyond secrets, who watches for attacks?

Azure has several security services whose names overlap, but whose jobs differ. Think in three stages: prevent, detect and respond. Prevention stops problems from happening. Azure Policy blocks bad configuration, and a web application firewall blocks common web attacks at the edge, such as injection attempts. Detection finds problems. Defender for Cloud assesses your posture, flagging weak configuration, and raises alerts about threats. But detection does not fix anything by itself, so someone must act on its findings. Response is where Microsoft Sentinel fits. It collects signals from many sources, correlates them into incidents, and can run automated playbooks. It depends on being fed log sources, so it is only as good as what you send it. The table sets out each service's main job and what it is not. A web application firewall is not the same as application security, and a detection service is not a prevention service. Many plans bill per resource, so enable them by need. Product names and packaging change often, so judge each service by its job, not its label. When something does go wrong, what is the sequence?

Suppose an alert says Priya's account signed in from two countries within an hour. This is a containment problem, and the table gives the sequence. First, detect, which has already happened. Second, contain: revoke her sessions and disable her sign-in, so the access stops. Do this before investigating, because every minute of access is potentially more damage, and the logs will still be there afterwards. Third, investigate. The query in the card pulls her sign-in log for the last day, showing times, addresses and results, and the Activity Log shows what she, or whoever held her account, changed. Check what the identity could reach, which is the reason we use least privilege and time-limited elevation. Fourth, eradicate: rotate any secrets she could read and remove roles that were added. Fifth, recover, and then hold a review. A related question is patching. Azure patches the platform and the hosts behind its managed services. But you patch your own virtual machine guest operating systems, your libraries and your container images. That shared responsibility needs an owner. Next, preparing for the worst case: recovery.

Backups are the last line of defence, and they are the control teams most often assume rather than test. The mechanism depends on the data. Virtual machines use Azure Backup. Azure SQL takes automated backups that support point-in-time restore. Blob data relies on versioning, soft delete and optional backup, and file shares use snapshots. All of these bring back an earlier state, which is different from high availability, which merely keeps you running and faithfully replicates a mistake. Next, protect the copy. A competent attacker, or a careless administrator, will look for the backups. So keep them in a separate vault with its own access, make them immutable so they cannot be deleted early, and use soft delete to undo a removal. And finally, the part that makes a recovery claim credible: validate it. Restore to a new location, never over production. Check the data is correct, and time how long the restore takes. Write the result down. A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a control. With backups in place, we can set recovery targets.

Recovery planning starts with two numbers. The recovery point objective, or RPO, is how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. The recovery time objective, or RTO, is how long you can afford to be down. The table sets hypothetical targets by tier. The orders database might need an RPO of five minutes and an RTO of an hour, which suggests a geo replica and a tested failover. The shop site is stateless, so it loses no data and can simply be redeployed from code. And reports can be rebuilt from source, so a day is acceptable. Tighter targets cost more, so set them per tier, not for everything. Then order matters. Recover identity first, because nobody signs in without it, then network and name resolution, then data, and only then the applications, because each depends on what came before. Finally, some cautions. A paired region does not fail over for you. Capacity there is not guaranteed to match, you must design and test the failover, and failing back later is a second migration. Azure Site Recovery replicates virtual machines, but it does not cover every service. Last: quotas and throttling.

We end the chapter with the limits you will meet and the proof you need. Azure enforces quotas, which are ceilings per subscription and region, and services throttle callers who ask too fast, answering with a 429 status code that means slow down. Dependencies also time out or fail outright. The card shows retrying done well. Retry only transient errors, and wait between attempts with exponential backoff, which means increasing delays, plus a little random jitter, so a crowd of clients does not retry in lockstep. If the service sends a Retry-After value, honour it. Cap the number of attempts, and use a circuit breaker so a failing dependency does not drag everything down with it. Ask for quota increases early, since approval can take time. Most important, do not assume any of this works. Validate it. Load test at the peak you expect. Inject faults deliberately, with a service such as Azure Chaos Studio, to see how the system really behaves when a dependency disappears. And run a game day, where the team practises the runbook for a realistic failure. Resilience you have never tested is only a guess. With the system observable and recoverable, we can finally use the evidence to improve it.

Optimisation begins with measurement, and the first rule is to look at distributions, not averages. In the second table, the average response time for our product page on one day is a hundred and eighty milliseconds, which sounds fine. But the ninety-fifth percentile is six hundred and forty, and the ninety-ninth is fourteen hundred. Those slower requests are what some users actually experience, and the average hides them. Throughput matters too, meaning how many requests per second the system handles at acceptable latency. Next, find the bottleneck. The first table breaks one slow request into segments, with synthetic numbers. The browser to edge hop, our application code, even the catalogue call are all small. The SQL query accounts for three hundred and eighty of six hundred and forty milliseconds, fifty-nine percent. That is the first suspect. Tuning the render step, which is three percent, would be wasted effort. The method is simple: measure, change one thing, then measure again and keep what helped. Latency also rises sharply near saturation. And measure at realistic load, because an idle system hides contention. A fast database query needs fewer trips, which brings us to caching at the edge.

The cheapest request is one that never reaches your origin. An edge cache, such as Front Door, stores responses close to users and answers repeat requests itself. The table decides what may be cached in our shop. A product page is the same for every visitor, so it can be cached for a few minutes. An image, for a day. A cart is different: it is personal to one user, and must never be served from a shared cache, because one customer might see another's items. A write, like creating an order, is not cached at all. The cache key decides what counts as the same request. It usually includes the path and the query string, and sometimes selected headers. Include everything that changes the response, and ignore what does not, such as a tracking parameter, or you fragment the cache. Freshness is the cost. A long time to live means shoppers may see a stale price after a change, so choose a time that matches how often the content changes, and purge a changed item when it matters. After performance, the other half of optimisation is cost.

Cost optimisation starts with understanding where money goes, so list the drivers. Compute grows with the size of the machine multiplied by the time it is reserved. Storage grows with the gigabytes you keep, plus the operations you perform. Data transfer grows with the bytes leaving a region, which surprises people. Logs and metrics grow with what you ingest and retain. And idle capacity is simply headroom that nobody uses, which you still pay for. To attribute those costs, look at the right scope. Cost Management lets you view spending by billing account, subscription, resource group and by tag. Tags only help if they are applied consistently, which is why policy can enforce them, as we saw in the governance chapter. Remember what a budget is. It sends an alert as spending approaches a threshold, but it is not a cap, and resources keep running. Add anomaly alerts, which catch a sudden jump. Cost data also arrives late, so do not wait for the invoice. And review cost with the workload owner, since the owner knows whether a spike is a launch or a mistake. With the drivers known, how do we reduce them?

Rightsizing means matching what you pay for to what you use, and the first step is measurement. The table shows synthetic averages. One virtual machine sits at eight percent CPU, so it can be resized down. The production plan at sixty-five percent is about right, and we keep an eye on it. The development plan is idle at night, so schedule it off. And the database is spiky at thirty percent average, which might suit a serverless or autoscaling tier. The lever order reduces risk. Delete what is unused first, because it has no downside. Then resize and schedule. Then consider commitments such as reservations or savings plans, which trade flexibility for a lower price, and which should cover only load you are certain will remain. Re-architecting is last, because it takes the most effort. Sustainability belongs in the same conversation. Higher utilisation generally means less waste, because idle capacity still consumes resources. But a lower price does not prove a lower environmental impact, and operational limits, such as latency or availability targets, still apply. Next, comparing whole architectures honestly.

Which architecture is cheapest for our order API? The honest answer is: it depends on the load and the assumptions, so state them. The table compares three designs, virtual machines, App Service and Functions, in relative cost units, not prices. And it includes every line, not only compute: storage, data transfer, logs and monitoring, backups, idle capacity, and the time people spend operating it. Under a spiky load, Functions comes out cheapest, mainly because it has no idle capacity and little operational work. Virtual machines carry the most operations time, because someone has to patch and look after them. But read the numbers with their caveats, shown in the second card. A steady, heavy load shrinks idle capacity and can reverse the ranking. A strict latency target may rule out cold starts. And skills and migration risk are costs as well, even if they do not appear on an invoice. So the rule is to make the assumptions explicit, build the comparison with current prices and measured load, and revisit it when the load changes. Then, how do you actually move?

Moving a running system is a sequence of reversible steps, with one step that is not. The table lays out a staged cutover for the order API. First, build the new stack beside the old one. Second, shadow it: send it a copy of traffic and reconcile its results against the old stack. Third, send a small share of real traffic as a canary. Fourth, cut over, so the new stack owns the writes. And finally retire the old one. Notice the rollback column. Until the cutover, you can return easily. After the new system owns the data, going back needs a data plan, not just a redeploy, and after retirement you cannot go back at all. Plan for that point of no return before you reach it, copy data in bulk and then sync changes until cutover, and reconcile the totals. Expanding to another region is a design exercise too, not a switch, and failover and failback both need testing. Finally, record the decision. An architecture decision record, like the one in the card, captures the context, the decision and its consequences, and says when to revisit it. Months later, nobody needs to guess why a choice was made. The last section pulls everything together.

We finish by looking at the whole system, using the five pillars of the Azure Well-Architected Framework: reliability, security, cost optimisation, operational excellence and performance efficiency. The point of reviewing them together is that they interact. Making something more reliable usually costs more, and making it cheaper can reduce resilience. The first card lists one finding for each pillar, drawn from this course. Reliability: we have never tested a restore. Security: storage account keys are still enabled and bypass our roles. Cost: the development plan idles overnight. Operations: some alerts have no owner. Performance: one SQL query is fifty-nine percent of the slow request. Next, rank them. The table orders improvements by evidence and effort. Testing a restore is cheap and addresses an unproven claim, so it goes first. Disabling keys is also cheap. Indexing the slow query takes more effort but has clear evidence. Do the cheap fixes for proven risks first, and re-measure after every change. There is no universal best architecture. A design is good for a purpose, under stated assumptions. From here, continue with hands-on practice, current service documentation, and demonstrated deployment, security and recovery competence, because production responsibility needs more than following worked examples.
